Background (from the session that started this one):
JusPrin is a fork of OrcaSlicer (C++17, wxWidgets, CMake) on branch `jusprin-newui`. On 2026-10-24 Kenneth decided how every way of bringing a file into the app must behave. Today the Home page's "Import" button and a file opened from Finder both add the file into whatever project is open behind Home (since 2026-09-30 the most recent project always resumes at startup, so there is always one), a .3mf opened from Finder launches a second JusPrin process, and a .3mf dropped on a non-empty plate is silently cancelled because a 2026-10-01 change auto-answers OrcaSlicer's "open as project or import geometry?" dialog with Cancel. The decision: every way a file arrives starts a new managed project (Finder/Explorer open, a drop on Home, Home's button renamed to "Open…", File › Open Project), except a model file dropped on the Prepare canvas, which adds to the open project; a .3mf never goes through the project-or-geometry question; the app runs as a single instance; and a persistent "Add model…" button in the Plates and Project pane makes "add a part" discoverable, alongside File › Import (Cmd+I) and the Agent composer's + menu. The behavior is written in `agent-docs/jusprin/architecture.md` under "Opening and importing files" (with matching edits in `autosave-version-history.md` and `product-definition.md`), and a per-path code-change list is in `import-behavior-code-changes.md`. All four files are uncommitted in the main checkout `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin` and are not on any branch yet.

Task:
Implement the file-open and import behavior decided on 2026-10-24 so that it holds on every path through the app, and verify it.

Start by bringing the decision into your worktree: the three doc edits and the working doc live uncommitted in the main checkout. Run `git -C /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin diff -- agent-docs/jusprin | git apply` in your worktree and copy `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/import-behavior-code-changes.md` in as well. Read `agent-docs/jusprin/architecture.md` › "Opening and importing files" for the behavior (the table and the rules under it are the spec) and `import-behavior-code-changes.md` for the per-path plan with file and line pointers. Read `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md` before touching any file outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`, and `AGENTS.md` for the build rules on the shared Mac (one build at a time, `-j4`, check `pgrep -fl ninja` and `uptime` first, never restart a running build). Do not touch `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin` itself beyond reading it and taking that diff.

The paths, and what done looks like for each:

1. Opened from the OS (Finder/Explorer double-click, "Open with", a second launch with a file): a model file opens as a new project named after it and the app goes to Prepare; a .3mf opens as a project and asks the existing "Previously opened file" question when it was opened before. One additive seam in `Plater::load_files(const wxArrayString&)` (a `set_external_file_open_handler` mirroring the existing `set_external_project_open_handler`), installed by `ShellController` with a routine modeled on `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter::open_project` (new project, drop unsaved preset edits, load, select Prepare). JusPrin runs as a single instance on every platform: `app/single_instance` must be true from fork-owned config code, and JusPrin's own Preferences window must not turn it off.
2. Home's button: rename "Import" to "Open…" in `HomeUI` (message type `import_project` → `open_file`, protocol, tests), `HomeBackend`/`HomeHost`/`OrcaHomeBackend`: the OS file dialog, then the same routine as path 1; cancel leaves Home as it is. Remove "+ New" from the gallery header (File › New Project remains). Home's empty state says "Drop a model or project here, or Open…". Rebuild the Home bundle after changing the page (see `agent-docs/jusprin` and the memory about CMake-built web bundles).
3. Drop on the Prepare canvas: a model file still adds to the open project; a .3mf opens as a project with no "project or geometry?" question (`project_load_behaviour` set to `load_all` from fork-owned config code; a fork-owned drop target replacing OrcaSlicer's `PlaterDropTarget` after install is the preferred way to keep "model adds" while path 1's seam exists — see the working doc for the trade-offs and the re-install at Plater.cpp:10095).
4. Drop on Home: spike first whether a `wxFileDropTarget` on `HomeWebView` receives drops over the web view on macOS; if it does, route to the routine from path 1; if not, implement the page-side drop described in the working doc and say in your report what the "Previously opened file" match can and cannot do without an OS path.
5. Add model… button at the top of the Plates tab of the Plates and Project pane (`Shell/LeftPane`), calling `Plater::add_model()`; sizes and colours from the design tokens through `ShellTheme` as `agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md` › "Writing UI code" requires, never a literal. An empty-plate hint on the Prepare canvas ("Drop a model here or add one").
6. Make sure nothing else in the app still adds a person's file into the open project behind their back: grep every caller of `add_model`, `load_files`, `open_3mf_file` and `load_project` in fork-owned code and in the OrcaSlicer entry points (`GUI_App::MacOpenFiles`, `GUI_App::post_init`, the `EVT_LOAD_MODEL_OTHER_INSTANCE` handler in `Plater.cpp`, `InstanceCheck.cpp`) and confirm each lands in the right row of the table. The Agent's `project_open` and `object_import` tools and the printer/calibration flows must keep their current behavior; run their existing tests.

Verification: update `tests/jusprin/test_home_host.cpp` and `HomeUI/src/App.test.tsx` for the rename; add shell harness checks in `tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp` for each path (an STL through the OS-open seam on a project with objects → new project id, one object, Prepare selected; a .3mf on a non-empty plate → the reopen question, not a silent cancel; Home's `open_file` with the dialog stubbed; the canvas drop target with an STL → object count +1, same project id) and keep the existing `external_3mf_*` and `--reopen-prompt` checks passing. Run the Catch2 suites you touched and the shell harness. Then prove it in the built app: build the worktree (the memory "Worktree build recipe" has the configure line that reuses the existing deps), run a copy of the app with its own `--datadir`, and exercise Finder-open (`open -a <app> file.stl`), a drop on the canvas, and Home's Open… button, reading the data dir's `log/debug_*.log` for which project each file landed in. Report what you could and could not verify live.

Commit on your branch with the three `agent-docs/jusprin` doc changes included; do not commit `import-behavior-code-changes.md` or any other working doc. Every OrcaSlicer-owned line you change needs the rebase note fork-stewardship.md asks for in the commit message. Done means: all six paths behave per the table, tests and harness pass, the live checks are reported, and the branch is pushed with a PR description that lists the per-path behavior and the upstream seams.

+Decided 2026-10-24. A file reaches JusPrin in a handful of ways, and they mean one of two things: **start from this file**, or **add this to the project I am working on**. +- Several files opened or dropped together make one new project holding all of them.
+- Opening a .3mf as a project is the only thing a .3mf does on the Prepare canvas. Wanting only the geometry out of a .3mf is rare, and the agent or File › Import can do it on request. +- G-code files keep OrcaSlicer's behavior (the G-code viewer) for now.

`agent-docs/jusprin/architecture.md` › "Opening and importing files" (2026-10-24).
This lists what has to change in code to make each path do what that section says,
with the file and function names as they are on `jusprin-newui` at a8a6139841.

## Where every path lands today

All OS and drop paths end in `Plater::load_files(const wxArrayString&)`
(Plater.cpp:14208), which adds a model file to the open project and sends a lone
.3mf through `Plater::open_3mf_file`. Home's Import button ends in
`Plater::add_model` (Plater.cpp:12613), which always adds. The agent's
`project_open` (OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:2498) already does "new project named
after the file, then load" and is the model for the shell routine below.

## 0. One fork-owned routine the paths share

`ShellController` (or a small fork-owned helper beside it) gets
`open_files_as_project(const std::vector<fs::path>&)`:

1. If `m_autosave` is missing or `m_workspace->tool_load_active()`, return false
   (a tool's own open is reported by the tool).
2. Split: a lone .3mf → `plater.open_3mf_file(path)`; with `project_load_behaviour`
   set to `load_all` (step 4) that reaches `Plater::load_project(path, "<loadall>")`,
   which runs the existing "Previously opened file" handler
   (`set_external_project_open_handler`, ShellController.cpp:435). Nothing new there.
3. Model files (one or several) → `plater.new_project(true, true, <stem of first file>)`
   (its autosave hook saves the outgoing project; `wxID_CANCEL` means the save failed,
   so stop and show the save-failed message as `project_open` does), then
   `plater.load_files(paths, LoadStrategy::LoadModel)` (the `std::vector<fs::path>`
   overload, which never re-enters the seam in step 1). Drop unsaved preset edits the way
   `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter::open_project` does.
4. `m_frame->select_tab(tp3DEditor)` when something loaded. The file-loaded report and
   the Agent's first message already fire through `FileLoadScope`.

Mixed drops (3mf + STL together): open the .3mf as the project, then add the rest,
which is what `Plater::load_files(wxArrayString)` does for `Multiple3MFOther` today.

## 1. Opened from the OS (Finder, Explorer, "Open with", a second launch)

Entry points, all OrcaSlicer-owned, all ending in `load_files(wxArrayString)`:

- macOS: `GUI_App::MacOpenFiles` (GUI_App.cpp:8601) → `plater()->load_files(input_files)`.
- Windows/Linux, app already running: `OtherInstanceMessageHandler::handle_message`
  (InstanceCheck.cpp:482) posts `EVT_LOAD_MODEL_OTHER_INSTANCE`; Plater.cpp:5444 handles it
  with `load_files(input_files)`.
- Any platform, launched with files: `GUI_App::post_init` (GUI_App.cpp:785).

**Seam (one, additive, in Plater.cpp):** mirror the existing project hook.
`Plater::set_external_file_open_handler(std::function<bool(const std::vector<fs::path>&)>)`;
at the top of `Plater::load_files(const wxArrayString&)`, after the path filtering, `if
(m_external_file_open_handler && m_external_file_open_handler(normal_paths)) return true;`.
The shell installs it with routine 0. Rebase note for fork-stewardship.md: the hook sits
before the `LoadFilesType` switch; a future rebase must keep it before anything that adds to
the model.

This single seam also catches the drop target (section 3), so the drop target must not go
through `load_files(wxArrayString)` any more; see there.

**Single instance:** `GUI_Init.cpp:48` reads `app/single_instance` from the config before
anything fork-owned runs, and `MacOpenFiles` reads it again at line 8603. OrcaSlicer's default is
false (AppConfig.cpp:171, Orca-owned). Options: (a) write `single_instance=true` from the fork's
earliest config touch (wherever `jusprin_*` config sections are first written; find it with
`grep -rn jusprin_agent src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin | grep set`), which takes effect from the second
launch and is zero lines in Orca files; (b) one line in `AppConfig::set_defaults`, Orca-owned.
Prefer (a) plus a first-launch write; note that JusPrin's own Preferences window must not expose
the setting, or must keep it on.

## 2. Home: Open… button

- `HomeUI/src/App.tsx:84`: label "Import" → "Open…", message type `import_project` → `open_file`
  (`bridge/protocol.ts:22`, `protocol.test.ts:24`, `App.test.tsx:203`). Decide the fate of
  "+ New" per the doc (remove from the gallery header; File › New Project stays).
- `Home/HomeBackend.hpp:33` `import_model()` → `open_file()`; `Home/HomeHost.cpp:162` routes
  the new type; `tests/jusprin/test_home_host.cpp:42` fake backend follows.
- `Home/OrcaHomeBackend.cpp:374`: replace the `add_model` call with: `wxGetApp().import_model(parent,
  input_files)` (the OS dialog with the model wildcard, which includes .3mf; GUI_App.cpp:4450),
  then routine 0 with the chosen paths; stay on Home on cancel. The "objects before/after" trick
  goes away; routine 0 says whether a project opened.
- Empty state copy on Home: "Drop a model or project here, or Open…".

## 3. Dropped on the Prepare canvas

`PlaterDropTarget::OnDropFiles` (Plater.cpp:4891) raises the window, selects Prepare, then calls
`m_plater.load_files(filenames)`, which after section 1 would start a new project for a model
file. Two ways to keep "model → add" on the canvas:

- **Fork-owned drop target (preferred).** After install, `plater->SetDropTarget(new
  PrepareDropTarget(...))` from ShellController. It raises and selects Prepare like Orca's, then:
  model files → `plater.load_files(paths, LoadStrategy::LoadModel)` directly (add, no seam);
  a lone .3mf → `plater.open_3mf_file(path)`; a mix → open the .3mf, add the rest. Orca re-installs
  its own target in one place (Plater.cpp:10095, inside the publish/reload path) — check that
  `set_external_file_open_handler` still yields the right result if that ever runs, or re-install
  the fork target from the same event. Lost: Orca's "drop one .svg to emboss" special case
  (Plater.cpp:4905), which the shell's hidden gizmo layer makes moot.
- Alternative: a `m_dropping` flag set by Orca's target and checked in the seam. Two seams instead
  of one; not preferred.

**No "project or geometry?" question for a .3mf:** `Plater::open_3mf_file` (Plater.cpp:14403) asks
through `determine_load_type` only when `project_load_behaviour` is `ask_when_relevant` (the
default, AppConfig.cpp:513) and the plate is not empty. Set the config to
`OPTION_PROJECT_LOAD_BEHAVIOUR_LOAD_ALL` from the same fork-owned config touch as
`single_instance`. The agent already flips this setting around its own geometry-only open
(OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:2535), so nothing else depends on the default. This is also what ends
the silent cancel introduced on 2026-10-01: with the dialog never shown, there is nothing for
`ScopedLeastChangeAnswers(prefer_cancel)` to cancel.

## 4. Dropped on Home

Home is a `wxPanel` holding a `wxWebView` (HomeWebView.hpp:30). On macOS the WKWebView takes
file drags itself, so a `wxFileDropTarget` on the panel most likely never sees them, and a page
`drop` event gives `File` objects without paths. Unverified; spike first:

- Try a `wxFileDropTarget` on `HomeWebView` (and on Windows' WebView2). If it receives drops,

# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

## Before you finish

A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:

1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.

   ```bash
   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
   ```

   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.

2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.

3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

## This fork's terrain

Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.

`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.

`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing

error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the

print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them

19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
needed edits across eight upstream files.

The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.

Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
page, silently.

Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
owned by Plater's event handler.

Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.

### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went

**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it

**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.

**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.

**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?

**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.

**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.

**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. # CLAUDE.md

JusPrin — a long-lived fork of OrcaSlicer (open-source C++17 3D slicer, wxWidgets GUI, CMake build system).

## Upstream vs. fork attribution

This checkout holds two codebases: upstream OrcaSlicer (the `upstream` remote, SoftFever/OrcaSlicer) and the JusPrin fork's changes on top of it. Fork changes include everything under `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/` and the seams the fork added inside OrcaSlicer-owned files.

- Say "OrcaSlicer does X" only for behavior upstream ships. Behavior added by a fork commit is "JusPrin does X", even when it lives in an OrcaSlicer-owned file.
- Check before attributing; the file path is not enough. Run `git blame` on the line, then `git branch -r --contains <sha> 'upstream/*'`. No upstream branch containing the commit means the fork owns it. Run `git fetch upstream` first if the remote may be stale.
- If you have not checked, say it is unverified whether the behavior is upstream or fork.

## Error handling discipline

- Do not catch an error merely because it can be caught. Catch only when the code can recover, translate the error at an abstraction boundary, or add context that is essential for diagnosis. Logging alone is not recovery.
- Represent expected states with normal control flow, not exceptions.
- Never turn an invariant violation or an "impossible" state into success or a silent no-op. Fix the invalid transition at the layer that owns the decision and let unexpected failures propagate to Sentry.
- Avoid duplicating defensive checks across layers. Keep lower-level operations strict, with their preconditions enforced by the caller that owns the workflow.
- If concurrency makes an invalid state reachable, fix the ordering or synchronization instead of suppressing the resulting error.
- Suppress an error only when it is genuinely expected and safely recoverable; document the reason and cover it with a test. Never broadly swallow unexpected errors.
- Prefer removing the root cause over reducing the visibility of its symptoms. Tests should encode valid transitions and assert that invalid ones remain visible.

## Build Commands

```bash
# macOS
cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo --target all --

# Linux
cmake --build build --config RelWithDebInfo --target all --

# Windows (replace %build_type% with Debug/Release/RelWithDebInfo)
cmake --build . --config %build_type% --target ALL_BUILD -- -m
```

Node/npm is required to build the Agent and Home pages, or configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF` and supply the bundles.

### Building on a shared machine

Several agent sessions build on the same Mac at once. Without a limit, ninja runs one compile job per core plus two, so every build you start can take the whole machine. In 2026-10 one session stacked four builds in one build directory: 56 clang processes on 12 cores. It kept restarting its build to change targets and never limited the job count.

- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. If the load is already above the core count, wait or build less.
- Limit jobs: `cmake --build … -- -j4`.
- Decide the full target list before starting. Never restart a running build to add or change targets: let it finish, then build the rest.
- Run one build per build directory. Two ninja processes in one directory compete and can leave its records inconsistent.
- Stopping a build means stopping ninja. `pkill -f "cmake --build …"` kills only the cmake wrapper, and ninja keeps compiling. Start long builds in their own process group (`perl -e 'setpgrp(0,0); exec @ARGV' cmake --build …`) and stop them with `kill -- -<pgid>`. Then confirm with `pgrep -fl ninja` before building again.
- When a build is slow, count your own compile processes before blaming the load on other sessions.
- Reuse an existing build where the task allows. Ask before configuring a fresh full-app build the task does not require.

## Testing

Catch2 framework. Tests in `tests/` directory.

```bash
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure           # all tests
ctest --test-dir ./tests/libslic3r              # individual suite
ctest --test-dir ./tests/fff_print
```

Printer UI without hardware: `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md` (Bambu in-process fake). Isolated `--datadir`; do not drive another JusPrin instance.

## Code Style

- C++17, selective C++20. PascalCase classes, snake_case functions/variables
- `#pragma once` for headers. Smart pointers and RAII preferred
- Parallelization via TBB — be mindful of shared state

## Key Entry Points

- App startup: `src/OrcaSlicer.cpp`
- Slicing pipeline: `src/libslic3r/Print.cpp`
- All print/printer/material settings: `src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp`
- GUI: `src/slic3r/GUI/`
- Core algorithms: `src/libslic3r/` (GCode/, Fill/, Support/, Geometry/, Format/, Arachne/)
- Printer profiles: `resources/profiles/[manufacturer].json`

## JusPrin Production UI

- Start with `agent-docs/jusprin/README.md` for the canonical product definition, production architecture, verification method, Orca integration guidance, and design system.
- Before editing any file outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`, read `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md`. Every line changed in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase, so those changes must be small, product-neutral, additive where possible, and accompanied by the rebase evidence that document requires.
- Experimental plans, probes, screenshots, logs, and temporary UI code remain on `jusprin-v2-poc`. Use `agent-docs/jusprin/poc-reference.md` for exact commit and path pointers; do not cherry-pick the POC wholesale.
- Curated brand and semantic UI assets live under `resources/jusprin/`.
- Before writing or changing any UI code, native or Agent page, follow "Writing UI code" in `agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md`: every color, radius, font, and control size comes from the token file through `ShellTheme`, the shell recipes, or the CSS variables. A value with no token gets a token and a guard first, never a literal.
- Temporary working docs (handoffs, findings, plans written for another agent) stay untracked: never commit them, and never add them to `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude`. Untracked files in `git status` are how Kenneth tracks work that isn't finished.

## Critical Constraints

- **Backward compatibility required** for .3mf project files and printer profiles
- **Cross-platform** — all changes must work on Windows, macOS, and Linux
- Profile/format changes need version migration handling
- Dependencies built separately in `deps/build/`, then linked to main app

## Code review focus areas

- Changes must not cause regressions in existing functionality, defaults, profiles, or project compatibility.
- Features gated by options must not affect existing behavior when those options are disabled.
- Changes should follow the existing code style and architecture. Architectural changes should be justified in code comments and the PR description.
- Add helper functions or utilities only when existing code cannot reasonably be reused. Avoid duplication.
- Changes to OrcaSlicer-owned files must be additive where possible. Rewriting an upstream function, or reimplementing upstream behavior beside it, needs explicit justification in the PR description.
- When an upstream line is deleted or relocated, say where it went and what a future rebase must carry into the new home.
- Keep code concise and clear. Manually simplify AI generated bloated codes before review.
- Include targeted tests or documented verification for behavior changes, especially in slicing logic, profiles, formats, and GUI defaults.

On 2026-10-21 Kenneth found 4 Release builds and 56 clang processes on 12 cores, all mine, in one worktree. Every ninja ran at its default -j (cores + 2), so 4 × 14 = 56. He pointed out that the orphaned processes were the smaller problem. The bigger one was that I put that many builds there at all.

What I did wrong, in order of weight:
1. I treated builds as free on a machine other sessions build on too. I never passed `-j`. I saw load 33, then 76, and started more builds anyway.
2. I restarted the build three times to change its target list or to slip in a small target. Each restart cost a full set of jobs. Waiting for the running build and adding targets afterwards cost nothing.
3. I went against the brief ("reuse the existing build; another session may be building") by configuring a fresh full-app build for an optional live check.
4. I blamed the slowness on "other sessions" without counting my own processes. That is the plausible-story-instead-of-checking failure from CLAUDE.md.
5. Mechanism: `pkill -f "cmake --build <dir>"` kills only the wrapper. Its `ninja -C <dir>` child keeps compiling as an orphan. I never checked that a stop had worked.

**Why:** the machine is shared. My extra jobs slow every other session, and two ninjas in one build dir can leave its records inconsistent.

**How to apply:**
- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. Cap jobs with `-- -j4` (fewer when load is above the core count).
- Decide the full target list once. Never restart a build to change it.
- Run one build per dir as its own process group (`set -m`, then kill with `kill -- -<pgid>`). After any stop, confirm with `pgrep -fl "ninja.*<dir>"`.
- Ask before a full-app build that the task did not require.

Related: [[background-bash-timeout-kills-builds]], [[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]], [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

## Writing UI code

Rules for anyone, human or agent, adding or changing a JusPrin surface. They
exist because every value that is typed by hand drifts from the design system and
from the other side of the app within weeks; today's guards catch most of it, but
only if the code goes through the token file in the first place.

1. **Never type a color, radius, font, or control size.** Every one comes
   from `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`. Native code reads it
   through `ShellTheme`: `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for radii,
   spacing, and per-component sizes, `font(role)` for type. A stock
   `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button` is
   dressed through `Shell/ShellRecipes.hpp`, never by calling its setters
   with literals. The Agent page uses only `var(--…)`: `--<group>-<name>` for
   color, `--radius-<name>`, `--font-<role>`, `--font-code`, and
   `--button-<recipe>-padding`.
2. **If the value you need has no token, add the token first.** Put it in
   the JSON, extend the guard in `tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp` so a
   later edit cannot silently move it, then read it from code. Do not write
   the number "for now": the guards cannot see a literal that is already
   there, and the next reader cannot tell a decision from an accident. A
   value that exists in the design artifacts but not in the roles or scales is a design
   decision to raise, not a reason to type it.
3. **Layout spacing may stay literal, on the scale.** Padding between
   regions, gaps, and margins use 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, or 48 DIP.
   Control padding is not layout spacing; it comes from a button recipe.
4. **Pick the nearest role, never a bespoke size.** The roles are the whole
   type system. Bold at a body or label size is a role of its own; if a
   surface seems to need a size that no role has, see rule 2.
5. **The design system wins when it and the code disagree.** The two Claude
   artifacts are the source of truth (Kenneth, 2026-10-20; Figma is
   retired): the Design System
   (https://claude.ai/artifact/3zgiix8rAw3rXextQnR5UL) and the "JusPrin v2"
   canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v). Change the
   token file to match, or, when the code's value is the one to keep, change
   the artifact first. Do not trust old commit messages about either.
6. **Run the guards before calling UI work done:** `brand_tokens_tests`,
   `shell_theme_tests`, and `npm test` in `AgentUI`. Then look at the surface
   in the running app; the guards prove the code went through the tokens,
   not that the result looks right.
7. **Upstream files are off limits for style.** OrcaSlicer's own screens are
   retinted through the hooks `BrandPalette.cpp` installs and nothing else;
   see [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). Their radii and fonts stay
